common_name: Dr. W. Van Fleet Rose (Once-Blooming Parent of New Dawn)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring against a sturdy support structure; Dr. W. Van Fleet needs a substantial fence, arbor, or pergola capable of supporting a large, vigorous climber for decades.

directions: Dr. W. Van Fleet was introduced in 1910 by its namesake USDA hybridizer, who crossed Rosa wichurana with hybrid tea and tea rose parentage to breed an unusually vigorous, cold-hardy climber for its era. The long, arching canes produce one spectacular late-spring flush of large, high-centered, soft pink, double flowers carrying a strong sweet fragrance, after which the plant rests rather than reblooming. A 1930 bud sport found on a New Jersey plant repeated its bloom through the season; patented in 1931 as 'New Dawn', it became famous as the first plant ever granted a United States patent. Train the long canes horizontally along a fence or trellis to encourage lateral flowering shoots, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood immediately after the spring bloom.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Climbing Iceberg Rose (Climbing Sport of the White Floribunda Iceberg)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun against a fence, arbor, or pillar; Climbing Iceberg needs tying in to its support since it does not climb by itself.

directions: Climbing Iceberg arose as a natural bud sport discovered in 1968 on the classic white floribunda Iceberg, retaining the same pure white, lightly fragrant, cupped flowers borne in large clusters above glossy, light-green foliage. Like most climbing sports of floribunda roses, it produces its heaviest flush in spring, with lighter, scattered repeat bloom through summer and fall rather than the near-continuous cycle of the bush form. The long, pliable canes can reach 12 to 15 feet and need tying to a fence, arbor, or pillar as they grow. Prune only lightly right after the main spring flush, removing spent wood but leaving the older cane framework intact, since heavy winter pruning removes the following year's flowering wood.
sources: World Federation of Rose Societies — Rose Hall of Fame

common_name: Royal Gala Apple (Deeper-Red Striped Sport of Gala)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; in zone 8-9 plant December-February. Royal Gala requires the same 500-600 chill hours as standard Gala. Plant with a compatible cross-pollinator (Fuji, Honeycrisp, Granny Smith) within 50 feet for good fruit set.

directions: Royal Gala arose in New Zealand as a more deeply and evenly colored bud sport of the original Gala apple, showing bright red striping over a larger portion of the fruit's surface than the parent strain. It colors reliably even in seasons with less pronounced day-night temperature swings, which made it the preferred strain for commercial orchards worldwide — most apples sold simply as 'Gala' in supermarkets today are actually the Royal Gala strain rather than the original 1934 release. Flavor, texture, and chill requirement are essentially identical to standard Gala: crisp, fine-grained, sweet, and low in acidity, with fruit ripening in the early-to-mid season. Provide a compatible pollinizer such as Fuji or Golden Delicious within about 50 feet for reliable fruit set.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Research and Extension Center
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Apple Variety Selection for Texas

common_name: Thompson Pink Grapefruit (Original 1913 Pink-Fleshed Sport of Marsh)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; grapefruit trees are large and require adequate space (20-25 feet diameter at maturity); Thompson Pink is self-fruitful and productive without a pollinator.

directions: Thompson Pink was discovered in 1913 in Oneco, Florida as a pink-fleshed bud sport growing on a branch of an otherwise ordinary white Marsh grapefruit tree, making it the first commercially propagated pink grapefruit. The fruit matches Marsh in size, seediness, and tree habit, but the flesh carries a soft pink blush from pigment accumulation rather than the pale cream of the parent, with a similar balanced sweet-tart flavor. Thompson Pink became the direct ancestor of the deeper-colored Ruby Red, discovered as a further bud sport in Texas in 1929, and stands behind most pink and red grapefruit grown commercially today. Grow it exactly as Marsh grapefruit, in full sun on well-drained soil, and expect fruit to hold well on the tree through winter without losing quality.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Lion Head Camellia (Historic Yunnan Reticulata, Shi Zi Tou)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Lion Head is an old Yunnan reticulata cultivar used as a breeding parent for many later large-flowered hybrids.

directions: Lion Head, known in China as Shi Zi Tou, is one of the historic old Yunnan reticulata camellias grown in temple and courtyard gardens for generations before entering Western cultivation in the twentieth century alongside sister heirlooms such as 'Captain Rawes' and 'Crimson Robe'. Its large, loosely semi-double flowers open deep rose-red with heavily textured, irregular petals surrounding a prominent boss of golden stamens, giving the bloom a shaggy, informal character typical of the oldest reticulata cultivars. Because of its large flower size and vigorous constitution, Lion Head was used extensively as a breeding parent for later reticulata hybrids, including 'William Hertrich' at San Marino's Huntington Gardens. Like other reticulatas it is less cold-hardy and more open in habit than japonica camellias, so site it in a sheltered spot with acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and afternoon shade.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ure was bred for the extreme winter cold of the Canadian Prairies and needs a second Ussurian-derived pear nearby for pollination.

directions: Ure was bred in Manitoba at Canada's Morden Research Station from Ussurian pear parentage crossed with a European pear, combining the species' extreme cold hardiness with noticeably better fruit size and quality than straight Pyrus ussuriensis selections. Trees survive winter temperatures well below -40 degrees F and set reliable crops even in the short growing seasons of the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, where standard European pear cultivars cannot be grown at all. The medium-sized, yellow-green fruit has a mild, sweet flavor acceptable for fresh eating when fully ripe, though most growers favor it for canning, sauce, and preserves like other ultra-hardy prairie pears. Plant with a second Ussurian-derived pear such as 'Rescue' for best pollination, and expect a vigorous, disease-resistant tree that needs little spraying even in humid climates.

common_name: Rescue Pear (Early Canadian Cold-Hardy Prairie Pear)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Rescue is one of the earliest cold-hardy pear cultivars bred from Ussurian pear parentage and needs a second hardy pear nearby for pollination.

directions: Rescue was one of the earliest cold-hardy pear cultivars bred in Canada from Ussurian pear parentage, selected specifically to survive prairie winters that kill standard European pear cultivars outright. It blooms later than most pears in spring, helping its flowers escape many late-frost events that damage earlier-blooming fruit trees in northern climates. The medium, round, yellow-green fruit ripens in late summer with a mild, somewhat gritty texture better suited to canning, sauce, and preserves than fresh eating, though well-ripened fruit softens to acceptable fresh dessert quality. Like other Ussurian-derived pears, Rescue shows good resistance to fire blight, an important advantage over European pears in humid growing regions, and benefits from a second cold-hardy pear such as 'Ure' planted nearby for cross-pollination.
